3.4A Integrity Anchor and Canonical Freeze Surface When an ID_3 inspection cycle reaches freeze state, a deterministic canonical surface is produced.

The canonical freeze surface contains: • session_baseline.canonical.json • session_variant.canonical.json • module_03_baseline.canonical.json • module_03_variant.canonical.json • hashes.txt These artifacts represent the structurally aligned, inspection-ready versions of the selected ID_2 records.
The file hashes.txt serves as the deterministic integrity anchor for the frozen pack.
Freeze integrity is therefore anchored at the canonical layer, not at the working layer.

rules: Once an artifact pack enters frozen_under_ID_3 state: • it is immutable as issued, • it may not revert to corrected in-place, • it may not silently re-enter operational posture.
If revision is required: • a new ID_3 inspection cycle must be initiated, or • the frozen pack may be copied into a new ID_2 session with a new session identifier.
All transitions must be explicit and logged.

rules: Abstract As artificial intelligence systems scale in autonomy, capability, and societal reach, governance approaches based on static compliance, documentation, and post-hoc audits do not provide lifecycle assurance.
CSC assurance shall be derived exclusively from observed system behavior, rather than declarative compliance statements or static documentation.
As a result, governance approaches that rely primarily on documentation, one-time assessments, or post-hoc audits do not provide meaningful lifecycle assurance.

While such mechanisms may provide baseline accountability at a point in time, they do not provide lifecycle assurance for systems that: • are retrained, fine-tuned, or updated after deployment, • incorporate third-party models, tools, or data sources, • operate across heterogeneous environments and jurisdictions, or • exhibit emergent behavior through interaction with users and other systems.
Static compliance frameworks shall not be considered sufficient to demonstrate ongoing conformity with safety, ethical, or regulatory expectations.
Attestations assert intent or design, but they do not verify behavior.
Trust engineering shall be grounded in telemetry that reflects how an AI system actually behaves under simulation and during runtime operation.

Within this framework: • governance claims shall be supported by measurable evidence; • assurance shall be revocable when evidence degrades; and • trust shall be earned continuously, not granted indefinitely.
constraints: Contemporary AI systems are adaptive, probabilistic, and increasingly composed of multiple models, tools, and services, introducing risks that cannot be adequately managed through point-in-time assessment alone.

Access PoD shall function as a continuous control system, rather than a static compliance mechanism, enabling real-time oversight, proportional intervention, and telemetry-based assurance.
4.1 Policy-as-Code and Runtime Enforcement Within the Access PoD framework, governance policies shall be implemented as executable policy-as- code artifacts.
These policies shall be enforceable at runtime, rather than relying on external procedures or post-hoc review.

Policy-as-code shall: • define allowable and disallowed system behaviors; • specify thresholds for intervention and escalation; • encode sector-specific and context-specific constraints; and • produce machine-readable outcomes for audit and assurance.
The Access PoD engine shall explicitly govern delegation boundaries between internal and external components.

Delegation controls shall: • identify whether a model or service is internal or external; • specify permitted scopes of interaction and data exchange; • enforce policy constraints prior to and after delegation; and • capture telemetry associated with delegated actions.

Where external models are used, the Access PoD engine shall maintain governance visibility and accountability for outcomes within the defined scope of use.

Page | 14 4.3 Enforcement Points as Control Objectives Access PoD shall enforce policies at defined enforcement points, each of which constitutes a control objective for governance and assurance purposes.

Enforcement points shall include where applicable: • inference and decision gateways; • tool invocation and action execution boundaries; • data access, transformation, and transfer interfaces; • human-in-the-loop review and escalation queues; and • model update, retraining, and configuration change events.
Each enforcement point shall be uniquely identifiable, policy-addressable, and auditable.
Failure to enforce policy at a defined enforcement point shall be treated as a control failure for assurance and scoring purposes.

4.4 Telemetry Capture and CSC Evidence Alignment Telemetry captured by the Access PoD engine shall form the primary evidence base for CSC scoring and certification.

Telemetry shall: • be structured and machine-readable; • be attributable to specific enforcement points and policy controls; • include timestamps, decision outcomes, and contextual metadata; and • support traceability across system components and lifecycle events.
Telemetry capture shall be continuous and shall not be selectively enabled solely for certification events.
Where telemetry is incomplete, degraded, or unavailable, CSC scoring shall be constrained or suspended accordingly.

A CSC does not represent a point-in-time approval and shall not remain valid in the absence of supporting evidence.

The CSC lifecycle shall include, at a minimum: • issuance based on sufficient telemetry; • continuous re-evaluation as new telemetry is generated; • downgrade where evidence indicates increased risk or control degradation; • suspension where evidence is incomplete or unreliable; and • revocation where critical governance failures are identified.
Revocation shall not be treated as punitive.
Re-issuance shall require renewed evidence, not administrative reinstatement.
5.4 Avoiding Certification-as-Status Ambiguity CSC shall not be treated as a status badge, marketing signal, or permanent designation.
Any use of CSC output shall reflect its dynamic nature and be accompanied by current risk interpretation.

Specifically: • CSC output shall not be cached or displayed without timestamp and validity context; • historical CSC levels shall not substitute for current assurance; and • changes in CSC level shall be considered material governance events.

6.4 Gate Conditions and Star Qualification CSC star levels shall not be determined by aggregate score averages alone.
Mandatory qualification gates shall be enforced to ensure minimum acceptable governance performance.

Scores shall be recalculated as new telemetry is generated, enabling detection of system drift, control degradation, or changes in operational context.

1.1 Why onboarding requires governance discipline Onboarding an AI system into operation is a high-risk transition point in the system lifecycle.
In many contemporary AI deployments, onboarding is treated as an administrative milestone- characterized by documentation reviews, sign-offs, or policy acknowledgements.
From the perspective of this framework: • onboarding precedes alignment maturity; • operational behavior is not yet fully understood; and • risk profiles are provisional and subject to change.

Without governance discipline at onboarding, organizations may inadvertently: • assert trust before evidence exists, • conflate readiness with compliance, • or allow systems to operate without effective containment mechanisms.

8.1 What regulators can observe at each phase Regulatory and standards engagement during onboarding is necessarily phase-dependent, reflecting system maturity and governance readiness.

For under-defined systems, regulators may observe: • simulation-based risk discovery activities; • declared execution boundaries and enforcement intent; • existence of escalation and human oversight pathways; and • evidence that onboarding is constrained and exploratory.

For over-defined systems, regulators may observe: • sustained evidence continuity across lifecycle events; • stable application of runtime controls; • continuous assurance outputs derived from telemetry; and • observable degradation or revocation of trust where evidence warrants.
At no phase does onboarding itself constitute regulatory approval or compliance determination.

9.1 Treating onboarding as approval A primary failure mode is treating onboarding into a governance framework as an implicit form of approval, certification, or deployment readiness.
Onboarding establishes eligibility for governed observation, not endorsement.
When onboarding is misrepresented as approval: • risk is obscured rather than managed; • scrutiny is reduced at the point of highest uncertainty; and • accountability becomes diffused.
This framework explicitly rejects onboarding-as-approval.
Any representation of onboarding as certification, compliance, or regulatory endorsement constitutes a governance failure.

10.1 From onboarding to steady-state The transition from onboarding to steady-state governance occurs when runtime governance mechanisms operate reliably under normal and stressed conditions.

Indicators that an organization is ready to transition include: • sustained operation of runtime controls at declared enforcement points; • continuous, attributable telemetry across lifecycle events; • effective escalation and intervention under elevated-risk conditions; and • evidence that trust degradation or revocation has occurred appropriately when assumptions failed.
Simulation, runtime enforcement, and evidence interpretation continue, but onboarding constraints are relaxed in favor of continuous evaluation.

Non-exploitative by design Stress-testing shall not involve vulnerability exploitation, security bypass, or unauthorized access.

Reversible impact Stress-testing shall not cause irreversible system changes, data corruption, or real-world harm.

rules: Chapter 6 - Relationship to CSC, Trust, and Revocation 6.1 Why Stress-Testing Must Constrain Trust, Not Inflate It Governance stress-testing is often misinterpreted as a way to increase confidence.
Accordingly, stress-testing evidence may restrict, qualify, or delay trust signals, but it shall never be used to elevate trust status or justify deployment readiness.
Stress-testing outcomes do not: • increase CSC scores, • substitute for telemetry, • override CSC qualification gates, • or justify star-level progression.
• Degradation readiness Stress-testing may identify conditions under which CSC degradation or revocation must be triggered rapidly.
constraints: A governance system that performs well only under favorable conditions is not trustworthy, it is untested.
6.3 How Stress-Testing Interacts with CSC (Constraint Path) Stress-testing affects CSC only through constraint, not computation.

Document Scope This technical report deﬁnes a governance framework for dataset onboarding, lifecycle routing, and dataset passport metadata used in AI training environments.
The report establishes governance semantics and lifecycle principles but does not prescribe a speciﬁc machine learning architecture, training pipeline, or execution environment.

Execution systems such as Q-Pathformer or other training architectures may consume lifecycle- governed datasets produced under this framework, but such systems do not deﬁne governance authority within the Access-PoD model.

This document extends the governance framework established in APOD-TR-002 (Version A), the architecture illustration described in APOD-TR-003 (Version B), and the onboarding discipline deﬁned in APOD-TR-004 (Version C).

It introduces a dataset lifecycle and passport model designed to enable governed transformation of inspection artifacts and other structured records into machine-readable datasets for AI training environments.

Converting these materials into machine-readable training inputs introduces a governance challenge: provenance, authorization scope, and lifecycle constraints must be preserved while enabling controlled use in model development.
Page | 2 This paper introduces a governed dataset onboarding framework designed to bridge that gap.
Central to the approach is the Dataset Passport, a machine-readable declaration that records provenance, authorized use, and routing constraints for each dataset unit.
The model also introduces a multi-state dataset lifecycle in which datasets transition through controlled stages of evaluation, runtime use, and durable training eligibility.
This lifecycle prevents uncontrolled dataset mutation and ensures that promotion into persistent training corpora occurs only through explicit governance review.

While compatible with a variety of AI training environments, the framework may optionally interoperate with execution systems such as Q-Pathformer or other machine learning architectures capable of consuming lifecycle-governed datasets.

4.1 State 3 - Runtime and Synthetic Dataset Layer State 3 is the default entry point for newly onboarded datasets.

State 3 datasets commonly originate from sources such as: • inspection artifacts produced under governance workflows • simulation records or scenario analyses • operational logs and analytical outputs • newly ingested external datasets awaiting evaluation Because these datasets may contain contextual reasoning signals rather than validated training knowledge, they are treated as temporary or exploratory inputs rather than permanent training material.

Typical uses of State 3 datasets include: • runtime reasoning support • synthetic dataset generation • contextual memory structures • experimental training signals State 3 datasets remain traceable through dataset passports and lineage records, ensuring that their origin and authorization scope remain visible even during experimental use.

Dataset passports and lineage records maintain a clear record of how datasets were created, modified, and promoted throughout their lifecycle.
Third, the lifecycle model supports controlled dataset evolution.

Finally, the lifecycle framework allows AI training pipelines to incorporate diverse data sources without sacrificing governance discipline.

Under this principle, the presence of a dataset within the onboarding framework does not imply: • dataset approval • dataset certification • dataset trustworthiness • model safety • compliance determination • regulatory acceptance Datasets are treated as evidence-bearing artifacts, not authoritative knowledge sources.
Within the lifecycle model, containment is enforced through several mechanisms.

Second, datasets are routed through lifecycle states that separate provisional datasets from durable training corpora.

Third, dataset promotion into State 1 durable training corpora requires explicit governance authorization and the issuance of a new dataset version.

Page | 48 13.3 Three-State Dataset Learning Model Future research may further explore the relationship between the dataset lifecycle model and machine learning architectures.

One potential direction is a three-state dataset learning model aligned with the lifecycle states defined earlier in this document and conceptually related to the multi-state machine learning architecture described in Q-Pathformer research.
In such a model: • State 3 datasets function as contextual memory and exploratory signal sources during runtime sessions.
• State 2 datasets serve as a convergence layer where teacher and student signals are evaluated, validated, and organized before durable learning occurs.
• State 1 datasets represent curated training corpora used for refined fine-tuning of models under explicit governance authorization.

One potential approach is to maintain shorter context windows within individual lifecycle states while enabling larger contextual understanding across sectors or industries through aggregated datasets.

These methods may include: • periodic dataset promotion reviews • sector-specific dataset updates • governance-driven dataset revisions triggered by policy changes • controlled retraining of models using updated State 1 datasets.

Dataset Freeze Boundary (ID_3 Packaging and Archive Freeze) 12.1 Purpose of the Freeze Boundary This section defines the dataset freeze boundary applied within the Q-Pathformer DEV execution model.

The freeze boundary represents the transition from a governed dataset package assembled under operational reasoning conditions to a stable, inspection-ready artifact prepared for external interpretation.

This boundary is aligned with: the inspection posture defined in Access-Mode ID_3, the artifact lifecycle clarification described in APOD-TR-006-E.2, and the dataset containment and lifecycle routing model defined in APOD-TR-007.
The freeze boundary represents the final stage of the execution pipeline defined in this report, following: signal capture, dataset formation, dataset packaging, and pre-freeze preparation.

The purpose of the freeze boundary is to: preserve dataset structure and governance context as a fixed snapshot, ensure deterministic integrity through cryptographic hashing, enable inspection and review without altering dataset content or semantics, and prevent implicit authority or approval from being inferred from dataset completeness.
Dataset packages assembled under ID_2 operational reasoning posture remain non-inspectable until explicitly transitioned to ID_3 through the freeze boundary.
A dataset is considered frozen only when: it is prepared under ID_3 inspection posture, the artifact set is treated as issued for review, and further modification is suspended or versioned.

Conclusion 15.1 Summary of Contribution This technical report defines a structured execution model for transforming AI-assisted reasoning outputs into governed dataset artifacts within a lifecycle-constrained environment.

TR-008 introduces: a signal-first execution model, a tier-aware interaction structure, a governed pathway from signal capture to dataset formation, and an explicit freeze boundary for inspection-ready artifact preparation.

These elements collectively provide a disciplined method for: capturing reasoning outputs as structured artifacts, transforming signals into traceable datasets, applying lifecycle-aware routing and authorization controls, and producing inspection-ready dataset packages without introducing implicit authority.

It aligns with: Version A - governance authority and assurance semantics, Version B - execution boundaries and telemetry generation, Version C - containment discipline and onboarding constraints, Version D - stress-testing and ethical evaluation.
